sources: Condren, Mary. The Serpent and the Goddess: Women, Religion and Power in Ancient Ireland. San Francisco: Harper & Row, 1989, 66.

text: Ailinn, also spelled Aillinn or Aillin, was a princess of the southeastern province of Leinster. Her lover was Baile Binnbhéarlach, a prince of Ulster in the northeast. Each traveled to a trysting place midway between their realms. A fairy told the prince, falsely, that his lover was dead, and he died of grief at Baile's Strand, near the modern town of Dundalk. The fairy then carried the same story to Ailinn, and she too fell down dead of grief. From their adjacent graves grew two entwined trees, a yew from his and an apple from hers. Seven years later, poets cut down the trees and carved them into tablets. They engraved all of Ulster's love songs on the yew and Leinster's on the applewood. When the king of Tara, Cormac Mac Airt, held the two tablets near each other, they clapped together and could never again be separated.

okr.objective: Record Ailinn and her tragic romance with Baile Binnbhéarlach.
key_results: Show the fairy's deception, the two deaths, and the entwined trees and tablets.
